title: Review of Ti-6Al-4 V alloy processing, microstructure, and mechanical properties from powder metallurgy to additive manufacturing for engineering applications
abstract: Abstract Ti-6Al-4 V, a dual-phase (α + β) titanium alloy, has been widely used in aerospace, marine, and biomedical industries due to its outstanding properties, including a high strength-to-weight ratio, corrosion resistance, and improved mechanical performance. Because of these advantages, this alloy attracts considerable research attention, especially in enhancing its processing methods, microstructure, and mechanical performance. This review focuses on the processing of Ti-6Al-4 V through conventional powder metallurgy techniques such as metal injection moulding, vacuum pressureless sintering, microwave sintering and spark plasma sintering. The influence of processing parameters on densification, microstructural evolution and mechanical properties is discussed. This review examines advanced manufacturing methods, particularly additive manufacturing techniques such as selective laser melting, electron beam melting, and direct energy deposition, which enable near-net-shape fabrication and improved microstructural control. The role of post-processing, particularly heat treatment, in modifying the microstructure and enhancing the alloy’s mechanical performance is also considered. Overall, this review summarises the relationship between the processing methods, densification, microstructure evolution, and mechanical performance of the Ti-6Al-4 V alloy, providing useful insights for the development and application of this alloy in high-performance engineering fields.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Titanium (Ti) and its alloys are extensively employed in aerospace components - such as engine blades, fuel tanks, and structural sections, owing to their combination of specific strength, resistance to corrosion, fracture toughness, and stability at high temperatures [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. With a density of 4.43 g/cm³, titanium is as strong as steel, which has a density of 7.85 g/cm³ [ 1 ,  2 ]. Titanium is also among the most abundant metallic elements, along with iron, aluminium, and magnesium [ 2 ,  3 ]. To enhance its properties, titanium has been categorised by phase, such as single-phase (α alloys, β alloys) and dual-phase (α + β alloys). These alloys are designed to enhance the properties of pure titanium [ 2 ,  3 – 4 ]. However, pure titanium has limited strength, and demanding structural applications require alloying to enhance performance. Based on phase stability and alloying elements, titanium alloys are classified into three categories: alpha, dual phase and beta alloys. Each category exhibits distinct microstructural characteristics and mechanical properties depending on its stabilising elements and processing conditions [ 3 ]. Among titanium alloys, Ti-6Al-4 V (Grade 5 Ti alloy) is regarded as the most widely used and versatile grade, often termed the workhorse alloy [ 5 ]. It emerged in 1954 to stabilise the α and β phases by alloying aluminium (α phase) and vanadium (β phase), respectively [ 2 ,  6 ,  7 ]. The resulting microstructure of this alloy provides a better balance among strength, ductility and corrosion resistance, making it a first choice for aerospace, marine and other engineering applications [ 2 ,  3 ,  5 ,  8 ]. Over the past few decades, significant research has been carried out to improve the performance of the alloy through various processing and routes and optimising their processing parameters [ 9 ,  10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 – 14 ]. Among the conventional techniques, the powder metallurgical route provides better microstructural control, enhanced mechanical properties and reduced material waste. In addition to conventional routes, additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a promising approach for processing Ti-6Al-4 V components with complex geometry [ 15 ]. AM techniques such as direct energy deposition (DED), selective laser melting (SLM) and electron beam melting (EBM) enable layer-by-layer fabrication and reduce the material waste and time [ 16 ]. Furthermore, rapid solidification yields a refined microstructure and enhances mechanical properties [ 17 ,  18 ]. These advantages made AM-processed Ti-6Al-4 V an application in various arenas. Despite the extensive research from the literature, a comprehensive understanding of how a process influences the densification, microstructural control, phase evolution, and mechanical properties of Ti-6Al-4 V is still required. Therefore, this review aims to provide an overview of various approaches to processing Ti-6Al-4 V, particularly powder metallurgical routes such as sintering and additive manufacturing techniques, and to examine their effects on microstructural evolution, densification, and mechanical performance. The objective of this study is to analyse the reported processing parameters and their influence on properties, and to identify the optimal conditions to achieve better performance of the Ti-6Al-4 V alloy.

sections.heading: Production process of titanium
paragraphs: Various thermochemical methods have been employed to produce titanium from its ore, rutile, using reductants such as calcium, sodium, or magnesium. In Fig.  2 , these methods typically involve the reduction of TiO 2  or TiCl 4  [ 19 ,  20 – 21 ]. Kroll’s method, which was depicted in Fig.  1 , has been used globally by the industry until now [ 4 ]. In this method, titanium is extracted from the rutile ore form, i.e., titanium oxide. First, chlorination was performed, followed by the addition of magnesium to the TiCl 4  formed. By adding magnesium to it in an argon atmosphere at 1000 °C, MgCl 4  has been formed in a liquid state. Solid titanium was also obtained from this process after reducing Mg from it. Kroll’s process is considered superior for large-scale production due to its high purity yields and efficient recyclability of magnesium, which makes it more economical when compared to the sodium-based process [ 3 ,  22 ]. The Armstrong process typically involves sodium (Na) as a reductant, followed by filtration and distillation to separate sodium chloride (NaCl), and finally leaching and drying to isolate the titanium powder.
Fig. 1 Schematic representation of Kroll’s process [ 23 ,  24 ]
Fig. 2 Thermochemical reduction method

sections.heading: Titanium alloys and their applications
paragraphs: Titanium is a common material characterised by an atomic number of 22, an atomic weight of 47.9, and a melting point of 1668 °C. At room temperature, it crystallises in the hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure as α-Ti, and transforms into the body-centred cubic (BCC) β-phase when heated above 882 °C [ 25 ]. Some unique properties, such as specific strength, corrosion resistance, and fatigue resistance, make Ti and its alloys suitable for space, marine, and biomaterial applications [ 2 ]. Titanium is classified into several categories based on its phase characteristics and elemental composition. The classification of titanium alloys is illustrated in Fig.  3 ; the mechanical properties and applications of a few Ti alloys are reported in Tables  1  and  2 , respectively. Referring to Table  1 , alpha alloys have lower yield strengths, ranging from 170 MPa to 480 MPa. On the other hand, beta alloys have higher yield strength but are denser and may be more complex to manufacture due to the presence of more alloying elements. Compared to these alloys, Ti-6Al-4 V has higher yield strength (825–869 MPa) and a lower density (4.43 g/cm3), providing an excellent strength-to-weight ratio. The presence of both α and β phases in its microstructure contributes to better strength and ductility. Furthermore, as shown in Table  2 , this alloy is widely used in critical components such as aircraft structural parts, engine components and bio implants due to its reliable mechanical performance and biocompatibility. These advantages have made Ti-6Al-4 V a workhorse alloy among the titanium alloys.
Fig. 3 Classification of titanium alloy

sections.heading: α & near α alloys
paragraphs: These alloys are a class of Ti alloys, primarily composed of the alpha phase of Ti. The HCP crystal structure characterises this phase. These alloys exhibit better creep resistance, retain high strength at elevated temperatures, and possess good weldability. α-stabilising alloying elements such as Al, O, C, and N have been added to pure titanium, enhancing its properties. Both alpha and near alpha alloys have the same kind of alloying element but vary in quantity, meaning the near α alloys consist of 1–2% of β stabilisers [ 26 ]. Figure  4  depicts the microstructure of spark plasma sintered grade 2 pure titanium – alpha alloy at different temperatures from 750 °C to 1350 °C. The light region denotes α grains, which were segregated from the dark β grains. These alpha phases started to reduce when the sintering temperature exceeded the phase changing temperature [ 27 ].
Fig. 4 Optical microstructure of spark plasma sintered CP-Ti at different temperatures ( a ) 750 °C, ( b ) 900 °C, ( c ) 1050 °C, ( d ) 1200 °C and ( e )1350 °C [ 27 ]

sections.heading: (α + β) - Dual phase alloys
paragraphs: As the name suggests, this type of alloy consists of both phases in its microstructure, and compared to α and near-α alloys, it exhibits better strength. This alloy consists of specific amounts of stabilisers and exhibits HCP (α phase) and BCC (β phase) crystal structures. These alloys are heat treatable and exhibit a wide range of mechanical properties, including high tensile and fatigue strength, superior fracture toughness, and good resistance to creep and corrosion. Figure  10  depicts the microstructure of Ti-6Al-4 V (dual phase) alloy and its evolution with respect to the cooling conditions. These properties can be acquired by tailoring the alloy according to its composition and processing routes, which may differ due to the elemental composition, heat treating and cooling conditions [ 28 ,  29 – 30 ].

sections.heading: β - Beta alloys
paragraphs: Both the β and near-β alloys contain β-stabilising agents such as molybdenum, niobium, silicon, and manganese, but in moderate amounts for near-β alloys and relatively higher amounts for β alloys. The microstructure of near β alloys contains both alpha and beta phases, whereas β alloys consist almost entirely of the β phase. Both alloys are heat treatable and characterised by good toughness and high weldability. These beta alloys are applied where high specific strength is required along with toughness, especially in aerospace parts and high-pressure vessels, and are highly suitable for medical implants [ 31 ,  32 – 33 ]. Figure  5  shows the optical microstructure of the Ti-Nb-Zr-Mn beta alloy with altered Zr and Mn in different compositions. This microstructure depicts the dominance of the beta matrix in the alloy. GB denotes grain boundary in the image [ 34 ].

Fig. 5 Scanning electron microscope (back scattered) images of Ti-26Nb-xZr-yMn alloy. ( a ) x=4wt%, y=3wt% ( b ) x=7wt%, y=3wt% ( c ) x=10wt%, y=3wt% ( d ) x=4wt%, y=5wt% ( e ) x=7wt%, y=5wt% and ( f ) x=10wt%, y=5wt% [ 34 ]

sections.heading: Titanium-based shape memory alloys (SMA)
paragraphs: These alloys could return to their initial shape after undergoing deformation, often caused by stress or temperature changes. This behaviour is due to the reversible martensitic phase transformation, which enables the shape memory effect and superelasticity [ 35 ]. NiTi alloy is a popular choice among Ti-based SMAs and is renowned for its super-elasticity and shape memory effect (SME) [ 36 ]. However, the presence of nickel can cause toxicity over the long term in biomedical applications [ 37 ]. To address nickel-free alternatives to SMAs and mitigate the health risks posed by nickel, other titanium alloys, such as those containing vanadium, niobium, and other elements, are also being explored as shape memory materials [ 36 ,  38 ]. Unlike these functional materials, conventional structural titanium alloys, such as Ti-6Al-4 V dual-phase alloys, are used for structural components due to their high strength and good fatigue resistance, rather than their shape memory behaviour.

sections.heading: Overview of Ti-6Al-4 V - titanium alloy
paragraphs: The grade 5 titanium alloy has a two-phase (alpha-beta) structure. It contains 6% Al (aluminum) an α-stabilizing element, and 4% V (vanadium) a β-stabilizing element. At present, Ti-6Al-4V is the most widely utilised Ti alloy, accounting for more than half of all applications. It is favoured because of its outstanding properties, including biocompatibility, specific strength, heat and corrosion resistance [ 2 ]. For aerospace components such as fan blades and low-temperature disks, Ti-6Al-4V is a standard material for manufacturing. Since this alloy has a maximum temperature limit of approximately 315°C, it’s also suitable for the mid initial stages of compressor disks, which do not work at high pressure and blades [ 1 ,  3 ]. The microstructural characteristics of Ti-6Al-4V were strongly influenced by thermomechanical processing. The phase transition temperature of this alloy is 995°C; beyond this temperature, the microstructure may transform to the β phase [ 2 ,  7 ,  56 ,  57 ]. Cooling from the β phase can produce a range of microstructures, including equiaxed α, lamellar α + β, or martensitic α’ phase, which depend on the process and cooling conditions [ 58 ,  59 ,  60 – 61 ]. This range of microstructure may influence the alloy’s mechanical performance, particularly its strength. Beyond aerospace applications, Ti-6Al-4 V is used in marine environments due to its high corrosion resistance. The construction of pressure hulls for marine craft, including boats and diving vessels, necessitates the use of titanium alloys. As hydrostatic pressure increases by roughly 10 KPa per water depth meter, materials such as grade 5 Ti alloy and Ti-6Al-2Nb-1Ta-0.8Mo have become preferred. Deep-sea submersibles featuring titanium hulls can achieve operational depths of up to 6000 m [ 3 ,  5 ]. In recent years, increasing attention has been directed toward advanced manufacturing methods for producing near-net-shape components with maximum density. This dual aim offers significant benefits, from reducing material waste and production costs to facilitating the production of complex structural designs that exceed the capabilities of traditional processing methods. Although many techniques are available to achieve this for alloys such as Ti-6Al-4 V, this article highlights a few that demonstrate how these methods affect the alloy’s microstructural evolution and ultimate mechanical performance, illustrating their individual roles in advanced materials fabrication.

sections.heading: Powder metallurgy (PM)
paragraphs: PM is a cost-effective and efficient method for producing titanium alloys [ 56 ], especially when compared to conventional mechanical processes like casting, rolling, and forging, which are typically associated with higher costs, significant energy requirements, and excessive material waste [ 62 ,  63 ]. In powder metallurgy, key parameters such as the type and morphology of the powder, ball milling conditions, sintering temperature, and applied pressure play a crucial role. These factors significantly affect phase formation, microstructural development, mechanical properties, and material density. Optimising these parameters is essential for tailoring the material to suit specific requirements [ 64 ,  65 ].

sections.heading: Powder characterisation
paragraphs: In the powder metallurgical process, the powder type and its production route are important and play a vital role in densification [ 65 ]. Alloy powders can be produced by two primary methods: blended elemental (BE) and pre-alloyed (PA). Grade 5 titanium alloy was processed through the blended elemental method, in which mechanical alloying was used to combine commercially pure titanium (CP Ti) with aluminum and vanadium. For this method, Ti powder’s most common and cost-effective production is hydrogenated / dehydrogenated (HDH) [ 66 ], which is formed from TiH 2 . The TiH 2  compound is brittle and easy to crush while undergoing mechanical alloying to attain a refined size. While hydrogenated titanium undergoes sintering in a vacuum or controlled atmosphere, the hydrogen is removed, restoring ductility and improving densification compared to CP Ti powder. In grade 5 Ti, this HDH powder is also acceptable if the application demands it [ 67 ,  68 – 69 ]. J.-M. Oh et al. reported that when preparing BE powder through master alloys Ti-Al and Al-V, intermetallics may form at the sintering temperatures of 700 –900 °C, which affects density and properties [ 12 ]. Powder morphology is also a factor influencing the driving force for densification of Ti-6Al-4 V. José Luis Cabezas-Villa et al. reported that small-sized particles exhibit higher density than larger particles when sintered at the same temperature, and that the phase transition temperature also varies with particle size. Up to 98% of the theoretical density is obtained at 1100 °C, but the larger particle-sized sample did not reach the same density at the same temperature [ 70 ]. Like particle size, parameters such as compaction pressure, ball milling duration, and other process conditions also play vital roles in the material’s densification and property enhancement [ 13 ,  14 ,  71 ].

sections.heading: Conventional PM processing techniques
paragraphs: Powder metallurgy is carried out through sequential stages, including powder preparation, mixing, pressing, and sintering, the last stage. Each stage offers a variety of methods tailored to specific material properties and end-use requirements. The characteristics of metal powders, such as morphology, particle size, and purity, are primarily determined by the production technique used, which may include processes such as atomization, chemical reduction, electrolytic deposition, or mechanical alloying. To ensure a uniform mixture, powders are blended, often with additives such as lubricants or alloying agents that enhance the final part’s performance. The mixed powders are then compacted into defined shapes, forming the preliminary form known as the “green compact”, which can be created using metal injection moulding, uniaxial pressing, or cold isostatic pressing (CIP) / hot isostatic pressing (HIP). The next phase, sintering, involves heating the compacted part to facilitate bonding between particles through atomic diffusion [ 72 ,  73 ]. Modern sintering technologies, including microwave sintering (MWS) and spark plasma sintering (SPS), can significantly improve density, microstructure, and processing efficiency. Ultimately, the choice of processing methods in powder metallurgy is a key factor in influencing the final component’s strength properties, surface quality, and economic feasibility. A solid understanding of these processes is necessary for the engineering parts, which require high performance and accuracy.

sections.heading: Metal injection molding (MIM)
paragraphs: MIM is an advanced powder metallurgy process that merges the design versatility of plastic injection molding with the mechanical strength and properties of sintered material. Titanium alloys have been produced through MIM, particularly Ti-6Al-4 V for medical, aerospace, and high-performance engineering applications [ 74 ]. It is especially suitable for manufacturing small, complex-shaped metal components with tighter tolerances and high performance. The process is widely employed in the medical devices, automotive, electronics, and defence sectors because it can economically manufacture complex components on a large scale, compared to machining or casting processes [ 75 ]. The MIM process involves four main steps: (i) mixing or blending, where powder is combined with a thermoplastic binder system, named as feedstock preparation, usually made of waxes and polymers. This mixture is heated to form a homogeneous feedstock. (ii) injection molding - under pressure, the feedstock is heated to a partially liquid state and injected into the mold cavity. Once cooled and solidified, the part, known as a “green part,” is ejected from the mold. (iii) debinding involves removing the binder system, typically through thermal, catalytic, or solvent processes. After this stage, the resulting part, called a “brown part,” is porous and fragile but maintains its shape. (iv) sintering, where the brown compact undergoes sintering by exposing it to an elevated temperature in either a controlled environment or under vacuum, where particle bonding occurs, resulting in component densification [ 76 ]. The working of the MIM process is shown in Fig.  6 .
Fig. 6 Process flow diagram of MIM [ 76 ]

Zhengyang Mai et al. sintered Ti-6Al-4 V at three different temperatures, in the range of 1150 °C to 1250 °C, with an interval of 50 °C. The relative density of these samples was approximately 97%. The maximum density of 97.9% was achieved at 1250 °C. Along with the increase in sintering temperature, impurity contents such as C and O also rose, reaching 0.154% and 0.323% respectively at 1250 °C, which tends to enhance the mechanical properties [ 77 ]. In another study, Ti-6Al-4 V was sintered at sintering temperature parameters ranging from 1250 °C to 1350 °C in 50 °C increments, with holding times of 1 h, 2 h, and 3 h. The highest density was 97.9%, nd improved tensile strength was obtained at a sintering temperature of 1250 °C and a holding time of 3 h, which was concluded to be the optimal condition of the study [ 78 ]. Li et al. sintered Ti-6Al-4 V in different atmospheric conditions: argon and vacuum (< 10 − 2  Pa and < 10 − 3  Pa, respectively). Compared to argon, vacuum conditions (< 10 − 3  Pa) exhibited better properties. The density was similar across all conditions, around 97%, withthe vacuum-conditioned sample achieving a tensile strength of approximately 1022.7 MPa. In an argon atmosphere, TiC and TiO formations were observed. The sintering temperature for all conditions was 1200 °C with a holding time of 2 h [ 79 ]. In another study, Wanli Ren et al. investigated the optimisation of process parameters for Ti-6Al-4 V processed by MIM, with sintering temperatures ranging from 900 °C to 1200 °C in 25 °C increments. The holding durations were 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, and 4 h. The combination of 1200 °C and a 4 h holding time yielded a density of 97.5%, an ultimte tensile strength of 922 MPa, and a ductility of 12.8%. The poreevolution in MIM-processed Ti-6Al-4 V with respect to sintering temperature and holding time is shown in Fig.  7  as scanning electron microscopic (SEM) images. These images indicate that the density increased with rising sintering temperature, as shown by the porosity % for each temperature, which ranged from 26.7% to 9.65%. Neck formation between grains grew with temperature, increasing density and reducing porosity [ 80 ]. Points A and B are the locations that EDS measured, containing 82.87% and 80.2% Ti respectively. The authors reported that sintering Ti-6Al-4 V at 1200 °C for 4 h is optimal, as it yields better mechanical properties, including a tensile strength of 922 MPa and 12.8% elongation. Fom the reported studies, it was clearly observed that sintering temperature and holding time mainly determine density and mechanical performance. Higher temperatures increase density and cause grain coarsening, which may lead to phase transformation if the temperature surpasses the phase transition point. Grain coarsening can also affect the material’s ductility. They noted that to prevent the deterioration of mechanical properties caused by grain coarsening at high temperatures, it is advisable to sinter MIM - Ti-6Al-4 V at lower temperatures for longer durations, which can produce better overall mechanical properties performance. The summary of the reported sintering conditions, along with their porosity and mechanical properties, is presented in Table  3 . It shows that sintering at 1150 –1250 °C reduces porosity and increases strength. Holding time and sintering atmosphere also play a vital role in the material’s densification and mechanical performance. A longer sintering duration promotes diffusion and eliminates porosity. The high-vacuum sintering atmosphere (< 10^-3 Pa) exhibits higher tensile strength (approximately 1022 MPa). In practical applications, the MIM-processed components were used for small components. Binder is necessary for processing the material; porous Ti-6Al-4 V can be easily manufactured through this method, and it is highly useful in the medical field [ 81 ,  82 ]. Overall, the sintering temperature 1200 –1250 °C with holding time of 2 –4 h and controlled high vacuum atmosphere would exhibit balanced densification and mechanical properties of MIM-processed Ti-6Al-4 V. Residual porosity was a key limitation of this process, potentially reducing the material’s performance.

The following samples were sintered for the holding duration of 2 h at the sintering temperature - ( b ) 1100 °C, ( c )1125 °C, ( d )1150 °C, ( e )1175 °C and ( f )1200 °C [ 80 ]

sections.heading: Pressureless sintering
paragraphs: Pressureless sintering is a widely used technique for densifying powdered materials into solid structures by applying heat, typically below the material’s melting point, without any external mechanical pressure. Fine powders are first shaped into a desired geometry, often called a “green compact,” using methods such as uniaxial pressing. The green compact is then subjected to elevated temperatures in a controlled atmosphere (vacuum or argon furnace) [ 84 ]. A process flow diagram of pressureless sintering is illustrated in Fig.  8 . Several studies have investigated processing Ti-6Al-4 V using this method. These studies reveal that high temperatures are needed to densify the green compact, even when the particles are small [ 70 ]. Adjusting the material to meet phase requirements is difficult due to its low diffusivity during sintering. Figure  9  illustrates the microstructure evolution through scanning electron microscope images of the conventionally sintered Ti-6Al-4 V at varying sintering conditions temperatures, illustrating the material’s densification for the master alloy powder prepared by elemental titanium and Al: V, which obtained 97% of desity and a strong intermetallic was also obtained after the sintering temperature of 1200 °C [ 85 ]. In another study, Ti-6Al-4 V was conventionally sintered at 1150 °C, achieving 99.5% relative density and exhibiting improved mechanical properties using boron-enhanced (BE) powder. The density depended on the sintering temperature and properties, while the microstructure of other samples was influenced by the master alloy powder and various aluminum particle sizes [ 86 ]. Jianzhuo Sun et al. proposed a two-step sintering process that involves an additional heat treatment to improve density, called second-step sintering. The samples sintered at 1300 °C and 1250 °C achieved relative densities of 97.5% and 97.3%, rspectively with grain sizes of 136 μm and 135 μm, respectively. The sample sintered at 1250 °C achieved a relative density of 99% after a secon heat treatment at 1150 °C for 10 h, resulting in a grain size of 90.57 μm. The reduced grain size and improved density were attributed to enhanced diffusion and further pore elimination during prolonged heat treatment, whereas heat treatment at a lower temperature limited grain growth. Under these conditions, the tensile strength reached 968 MPa, elongating to 16.1%, demonstratin a synergistic improvement [ 87 ] in this work refers to the simultaneous achievement of high mechanical performance and ductility (16.1% elongation). This performance is influenced by microstructural refinement, which activates advanced deformation mechanisms, including dislocation cross-slip, in the stress-induced FCC phase, thereby relieving stress at the phase interface and delaying crack initiation. The process used a mixture of hydrogen and inert gas as the controlled atmosphere, with hydrogen partial pressure aiding densification. This hydrogen was subsequently dehydrogenated. The hydrogen partial pressure also induced phase transformations, a process known as hydrogen sintered phase transformation (HSPT), which combines conventional sintering in a hydrogen atmosphere with inert gas. Hydrogen plays a crucial role in both densification and phase transformation during this process [ 88 ]. The sintered alloy underwent various heat treatments in this study, and its properties and microstructural evolution were analysed. The microstructure exhibited different patterns depending on the cooling conditions, as shown in Fig.  10 . The as-sintered sample exhibited an alpha matrix with discontinuous beta trapped inside. Water-quenched samples displayed a bimodal structure, with approximately 40 vol% globularized grains, ultrafine acicular grains, and some elongated α grains with dispersed retained β. This condition exhibited the lowest elongation in tensile testing. Furnace-cooled samples showed a globularized structure throughout, with high elongation. Vacuum sintered (V.S.) samples had structures similar to those of the as-sintered and slow-cooled samples, featuring coarsened α-lamellar grains and continuous β layers between α. The water-quenched vacuum-sintered compact reveals elongated, fine acicular alpha grains with retained beta, but this condition did not yield the best mechanical properties. The studies clearly show again that sintering temperature was a crucial factor in densification. Achieving maximum density in processing Ti-6Al-4 V through vacuum pressureless sintering, like any other process, was not easy. Even though the sintering temperature is high, the material’s density is low. That elevated temperature may also lead to grain coarsening, thereby affecting the material’s strength. Post-processing, such as HSPT, can resolve the densification problem, but from a practical perspective, the material processed by this method is suitable for low processing cost, simple geometric complexity, and large scalability. The limitation of this process is that it is difficult to produce a fully dense material due to residual porosity and grain coarsening, which reduces its performance.

sections.heading: Microwave sintering
paragraphs: Microwave sintering is an advanced thermal processing technique that uses microwave energy to heat and densify materials. Figure  11  shows a schematic of a microwave sintering furnace. Unlike conventional sintering, which depends on external heating elements to transfer heat through conduction and convection, microwave sintering uses electromagnetic waves to interact directly with the material at the molecular level. This leads to rapid heating, shorter processing times, and often lower sintering temperatures [ 89 ,  90 ]. The heating profile of microwave sintering is shown in Fig.  12 , compared with that of conventional sintering. It requires lower temperatures to achieve equal or better densification than the traditional method [ 91 ].
Fig. 11 3D view and cross-sectional schematic representation of microwave sintering [ 92 ]
Fig. 12 Heating profile of conventional sintering and microwave sintering [ 89 ]

Using the MATLAB genetic algorithm toolbox, D. Singh and colleagues optimised the process parameters for microwave sintered Ti-6Al-4 V. Their study concluded that the sintering temperature was 1280 °C, the heating rate was 8 °C/min, and the holding duration was 78 min. These parameters significantly influenced the final density, compressive strength and volumetric shrinkage of the alloy. Additionally, the researchers reported that a slight reduction in the β phase occurred as the material was allowed to furnace cool from 1350 °C [ 93 ]. S.D. Luo and colleagues reported no significant difference in densifying the alloy through MWS compared to conventional sintering; the pre-alloyed Ti-6Al-4 V reached approximately 95% o its relative density even when sintered at 1300 °C, but the densification process was much quicker than with conventional sintering [ 94 ]. A graphical representation of the time taken to densify the titanium nitride compact between conventional and MWS is depicted in Fig.  13 , showing a shorter duration for microwave sintering (MWS) and a longer duration for conventional sintering (CS) [ 95 ]. In another study, the Ti-6Al-4 V composite was sintered at around 1600 °C; the sample’s porosity was 25%, possiblydue to the addition of carbon nanotubes. Phase analysis showed beta peaks along with TiC peaks; the beta peak may be attributed to sintering at the sintering temperature, and the TiC peak to the reaction of titanium with carbon nanotubes. These results highlight how reinforcement and elevated microwave sintering temperature influence porosity and phase evolution during processing of Ti-6Al-4 V composites [ 96 ]. Mahesh Mandapalli et al. processed Ti-6Al-4 V with a high-entropy alloy at 950 MPa, then sintered at 850 °C for 1 h. They achieved around 94% of the relative density across all samples and improved properties with composition [ 97 ]. From the reported study, it was evident that achieving maximum density with this process is superior to that of other conventional processes. The duration of this process is also short, resulting in grain refinement and strength enhancement. Even though rapid densification was achieved by this method, some studies reported that the density was around 96%, and that microwave energy absorption by the green compact was uneven, which may affect density and performance. Microwave sintering offers advantages in processing efficiency; spark plasma sintering may be preferred for a nearly full-density component.
Fig. 13 A comparative plot showing the densification time of Ti alloy under conventional sintering vs. microwave sintering [ 95 ]

sections.heading: Spark plasma sintering (SPS)
paragraphs: SPS is a modern powder consolidation process that has attracted considerable interest in recent years. In contrast to conventional sintering techniques, SPS applies uniaxial pressure combined with a pulsed direct current to achieve rapid heating and densification of materials. This combination results in shorter sintering times, lower sintering temperatures, and better control of microstructure [ 98 ,  99 ]. In this process, the powders were filled into a die that should be conductive, a pulsated direct current was applied, and uniaxial pressure was applied simultaneously to densify the powder. The process enables rapid densification through simultaneous joule heating and pressure, often without external heating elements. The electrical current generates localised heat at particle contacts, enhancing diffusion and mass transport mechanisms essential for sintering. The working of spark plasma sintering was illustrated in Fig.  14 . Unlike conventional heat flow, which comes from outside, and microwave sintering, where heat is generated inside the particles, the sintering mechanism in SPS is governed by a combination of thermal, electrical, and mechanical effects. The primary heat source is resistive, or Joule heating, which occurs when the pulsed current is transmitted through the graphite die, and when the powders are electrically conductive. This internal heating results in a uniform, rapid temperature rise, significantly accelerating atomic diffusion processes that drive densification. The mechanism of DC flow through the powder during sintering is shown in Fig.  15 . Simultaneously, uniaxial pressure is applied to the die while pulsed current flows through the powder. This combined action helps densify the material more quickly at a lower sintering temperature.
Fig. 14 Schematic representation of spark plasma sintering [ 100 ]
Fig. 15 Direct current flows through the particle in the SPS process [ 101 ]

Densification occurs rapidly through the SPS process; optimised process parameters are necessary to attain the desired properties. Several studies have been conducted to optimise the parameters for processing Ti-6Al-4 V to improve microstructural properties and mechanical performance. Suoqing Yu and other co-researchers reported that the optimal sintering temperature for Ti-6Al-4 V alloy using plasma rotating electrode process (PREP) powder with a particle size of 150 μm and spherical in shape. Their study involved sintering at five different temperatures, and they found that 925 °C yielded the most favourable mechanical properties. At this temperature, both the ultimate tensile strength and ductility exhibited balanced, enhanced performance, indicating a synergistic effect. The microstructural features of the sintered compacts at their respective temperatures were illustrated in Fig.  16  [ 102 ]. The densification achieved by SPS is better than that of other conventional methods; in this study, the maximum density was reached at 950 °C, which is below the transition temperature and lower compared to other processes. Microstructural evolution of Ti-6Al-4 V processed by SPS, shown in Fig.  14 , indicates that the compacts processed at 850 °C and 875 °C had low sintering driving force, leading to porosity, with relative densities of 92.2% an 96.1%, rspectively. The maximum relative density of 99.3% wa achieved when the compact was processed at 950 °C, indicating reduced porosity and maximum density. At 900 °C, an α + β duplex microstructure was observed along with β grain boundaries, with β grains evenly distributed within the α matrix. At 925 °C, a basket weave structure along with α colonies was visible in the microstructure. By 950 °C, a clear Widmanstätten structure was observed, along with grain growth, due to the increasing sintering temperature, with coarsened β grains contributing to lower strength compared to the 925 °C sample [ 102 ]. Other parameters for processing the Ti-6Al-4 V alloy, such as heating rate and compaction pressure, were optimised and reported in several studies to improve performance during SPS sintering of Ti-6Al-4 V. Dariusz Garbiec et al. studied and reported the optimisation of these parameters, finding maximum density at a heating rate of 300 °C/min and a compaction pressure of 25 MPa. These parameters yielded maximum hardness, elastic modulus, and overall mechanical performance. A detailed comparison of different heating rates and compaction parameter combinations studied in the research is presented in Table  4  [ 71 ]. Table  4  shows that an increase in compaction pressure from 5 MPa to 25 MPa − 50 MPa significantly increases the relative density, reaching full densification (~ 100). This may be due to better particle packing and reduced porosity. The heating rate also influences the alloy’s mechanical performance. Moderate heating rate around 300 °C/min with high compaction pressure resulted in enhanced densification and mechanical properties.

Ball milling duration is another key factor that significantly influences the processing and is also reflected in the properties. In a study by Yan Long and colleagues, the effect of varying ball-milling times on the mechanical properties of the Ti-6Al-4 V alloy was investigated. The powders were milled for 5, 10, 30, 40, and 50 h under an argon atmosphere, then compacted using the SPS technique. It results in an increase in milling duration, leading to a corresponding rise in compressive strength and, concurrently, an increase in interstitial elements. Notably, after 50 h of milling, the interstitial content more than doubled compared to the as-received powder. The authors identified a milling duration of 10 h as optimal, achieving a balance between mechanical strength and minimal interstitial contamination. Additionally, this condition provided improved plastic deformation and an around 99% relative density. Beyond this duration, grain coarsening began, which negatively impacts performance [ 14 ]. From the reported study, it was clear that it has better densification capability than other conventional processes, such as pressureless and microwave sintering. The rapid heating rates and applied pressure promote densification and grain refinement, thereby improving mechanical properties. In practical applications, SPS may be used for high-density components and where fine microstructure and improved mechanical strength are required. The limitations of this process were the geometric complexity; simple, structured components can be processed by this technique.

sections.heading: Structure – property relation in conventional powder metallurgy processing Ti-6Al-4 V
paragraphs: In powder metallurgy, processing parameters play a vital role in determining the alloy’s microstructure and mechanical performance. Following the individual analyses of metal injection moulding, pressureless sintering, microwave sintering, and spark plasma sintering, it is evident that all processes followed distinct routes for consolidating Ti-6Al-4 V powder. Differences in heat transfer and the applied pressure lead to variations in density, microstructure, and alloy performance. The main difference among these four processes lies in their densification kinetics. In pressureless sintering and metal injection moulding, the thermal exposure time is longer than in the other two processes. This would lead to the grain coarsening and the coarser lamellar structure. The geometric complexity of these processes was high with slight residual porosity, which leads to limits on better mechanical performance [ 26 ,  104 ]. On the other hand, microwave sintering and spark plasma sintering operate quickly, enabling rapid heat transfer. This rapid heating will accelerate the pore closure and minimise the grain growth. Below the phase transition temperature, nearly 98% of the rlative density could be attained. Compared with Microwave sintering and SPS, these methods maximise theoretical strength and refine the microstructure, while maintaining simple geometrical complexity. Table  5  shows a comparative analysis of these four processes in the structure-property relation. It summarises the processing of Ti-6Al-4 V through various conventional powder metallurgical routes. Among those, spark plasma sintering densifies the material more efficiently than the other processes because of its heating mechanism, but it has limitations in geometric complexity; simple components can be processed through it. In contrast, metal injection moulding was better at geometric complexity, but residual pores and shrinkage during sintering can affect densification, leading to property deterioration. Microwave sintering provides rapid heating, reducing sintering time, but non-uniform heating can result in improper density. However, the limitations related to equipment scalability and process control remain a challenge for large-scale industrial implementations.

sections.heading: Additive manufacturing (AM) of Ti-6Al-4 V alloy
paragraphs: Among the powder metallurgical routes, AM represents a major advancement in the production of metallic components. This layer-by-layer process forms complex geometries directly from metal powders, offering improved material efficiency and design flexibility. Unlike traditional methods such as casting, forging, and machining, which often generate a lot of waste, require lengthy processes, and require specialised tooling, AM delivers a near-net-shape method with shorter duration [ 106 ]. According to the ISO/ASTM 52900:2021 standard, additive manufacturing processes are categorised into seven types. Among those laser powder bed fusion processes, such as selective laser melting, direct energy deposition and electron beam melting, have been extensively applied to process titanium alloys such as Ti-6Al-4 V, resulting in refined microstructural features and improved mechanical properties [ 107 ,  108 ]. In additive manufacturing, selecting the appropriate processing parameters and building orientation in line with the requirements is vital for achieving the desired properties. Table  6  shows the properties of additively manufactured Ti-6Al-4 V alloy in different orientations.

sections.heading: Selective laser melting
paragraphs: In this process, the metal powder melts when the laser beam is applied to it. Then the metal powder starts to fuse, layer upon layer, creating a solid three-dimensional object directly from a digital 3D model, usually as a CAD file. A thin layer of metal powder, typically 20 μm to 100 μm thick, is first evenly applied to a build platform within a sealed chamber, often filled with an inert gas, such as nitrogen or argon, to prevent oxidation. Typically, a fiber laser is focused onto the powder bed, scanning in accordance with the cross-sectional geometry of the part for that specific layer. The metal particles melt and solidify wherever the laser hits, bonding to the layer beneath. Once a layer is finished, the build platform descends by a predetermined thickness, and a fresh powder layer is distributed across the surface. The laser subsequently scans the following cross-section, and this sequence is repeated layer by layer until the part is fully fabricated from the bottom upward. Figure  17  illustrates the working of the SLM process.

Process parameters are crucial in fabricating Ti-6Al-4V using SLM. Several studies have aimed to optimize these parameters for better material synthesis. H. Zhu et al. investigated how various process parameters, such as laser power, scanning speed and hatch spacing, were (240, 300, and 360 W), (800, 1000, and 1200 mm/s) and (0.08, 0.1 and 0.12 mm), respectively, affect the generation and evolution of residual stress in Ti-6Al-4V alloy. They reported that consistent parameter changes would not change the residual stress behaviour. However, scanning speed exerts the greatest influence, with laser power and hatch spacing having comparatively lesser effects [ 118 ]. J. Liu et al. studied how laser power and scanning speed influence the processing of Ti-6Al-4V through SLM. They varied the laser power at 70, 79, 88, 97, and 106 W with a stable scanning speed of 620 mm/s, then varied the scanning speed at 496, 558, 620, 682, and 744 mm/s. The highest density was achieved at 744 mm/s. Still, the optimal laser power was 79 W, as insufficient power leads to insufficient melting of the powder, while excessive power can cause aluminium boiling and disrupt the release of entrapped gas. They achieved a tensile strength of 1170 MPa and an elongation of 10% under two conditions. For condition one, the laser power and scanning speed were 79 W and 620 mm/s, respectively, and at 88 W and 744 mm/s. Under these conditions, both the α and α’ phase (which were limited) were more prevalent, resulting in higher ductility and fewer pores, contributing to improved properties [ 119 ]. The defects observed in samples processed under suboptimal conditions are depicted in Fig.  18 , (a) represents unmelted particles, (b) depicts crack-like pore defects, and the remaining two display deep pores. These defects resulted from non-optimal parameter choices and hindered the material’s performance. During SLM, solidification occurs very rapidly due to the high cooling rate. Due to this, the high-temperature β phase in the alloy transforms into a metastable α’ martensitic phase. This phase consists of a needle-like, fine acicular structure, which is not thermodynamically stable. The material should undergo heat treatment to decompose the α’ martensite into the stable α + β phase [ 120 ,  121 ] through diffusion alloying elements such as aluminium and vanadium. This phase transformation would improve ductility and reduce internal stress in the alloy.
Fig. 17 Schematic illustration of selective laser melting [ 122 ]
Fig. 18 Defects of SLM-processed Ti-6Al-4 V at non-optimal parameters (a) unmelted particles (b) crack like pores (c,d) deep pores [ 119 ]

T. Vilaro et al. studied heat treating the SLMed Ti-6Al-4 V to improve ductility [ 123 ]. After heat treatment at low temperature, ductility increased, and strength decreased. Similar to this study, researchers applied various heat treatment conditions to SLMed samples to enhance ductility [ 58 ,  77 ,  124 ,  125 ]. Through the HIP process, researchers achieved better ductility; Zemin Wang et al. reported improved ductility after subjecting SLMed samples to HIP at 920 °C and 100 MPa of pressure for 2 h of dwell time, then the samples were cooled by furnace cooling, resulting in ductility comparable to that of the as-SLMed sample [ 126 ]. Chunlei Qiu et al. also found that elongation was enhanced, and strength slightly decreased after HIP post-processing on SLM-processed Ti-6Al-4 V [ 127 ]. Along with these literatures, several studies were carried to optimize the parameters for processing Ti-6Al-4 V to enhance the properties [ 128 ,  129 – 130 ].

sections.heading: Electron beam melting (EBM)
paragraphs: This process is also a type of powder-bed fusion in additive manufacturing. This process utilises a focused electron beam as its primary heat source to produce fully dense metal parts. These procedures would carry out in a controlled environment to prevent oxidation and enable efficient electron transmission, making it especially suitable for reactive materials like titanium alloys. Initially, on the build platform, a thinner layer of conductive metal powder was spread evenly. The electron beam is applied to the entire layer for the pre-heating process at a lower energy level to lightly sinter the particles, helping to minimise powder displacement and residual stresses. After preheating, the beam selectively melts areas defined by the part’s CAD data, forming a solid cross-section. After each layer is finished, the build platform is displaced downward by a specified distance. The powder deposition, preheating, and selective melting cycle is repeated until the required shape is achieved [ 108 ]. Figure  19  illustrates the working of the EBM process. The high build temperatures typical of EBM help reduce thermal stresses, decrease distortion, and produce parts with excellent mechanical properties. Post-processing usually includes powder recovery, possible heat treatment, and finishing operations to achieve the near-net shape.
Fig. 19 Schematic representation of EBM process [ 131 ]

Several studies have been conducted on this technique to process the Ti-6Al-4 V alloy. Dana H. Abdeen et al. investigated processing parameters to improve density and mechanical properties. The analysis revealed that surface roughness and density are mainly influenced by offset focus. Increasing the parameter increases surface roughness from approximately 22 μm to 96 μm and causes a nearly 10% decrease in density due to increased porosity. Furthermore, surface roughness was also influenced by growing beam current and decreasing beam speed. This suggests that precise and uniform control over roughness and density can be challenging; a specific range of these properties can be obtained by carefully selecting parameters, especially offset focus [ 120 ]. L.E. Murr and co-researchers studied the microstructural evolution under the effect of cooling conditions in EBMed Ti-6Al-4 V in an argon atmosphere. These conditions included: a very rapid initial cooling from the melting temperature (approximately 1900 °C) to 700 °C (estimated at 10 3 –10 5  K/s), followed by a prolonged isothermal hold at 700 °C, and finally, gradual cooling from 700 °C to ambient temperature. over about 8 h after the last layer was deposited. Microstructure evolution revealed a very fine, generally uniform microstructure across the build. Key features included columnar grains of the prior β phase extending along the build direction. Within these columnar grains, typical (α + β) structures were observed, characterised by the Widmanstätten structure. Different-sized α platelets and β phase with rod-like morphology were forming at their interfaces. A distinct grain boundary (α-Grain Boundary) also formed around the columnar prior β grain boundaries. Dislocation density within the α grains was relatively low. The microstructure is shown in Fig.  20 . Regarding density, the study found spherical voids distributed non-uniformly across all samples. These pores occur due to argon (Ar) gas (used for the process that should be carried out in a controlled atmosphere) within the gas-atomised Ti-6Al-4 V powder [ 121 ]. The elongated columnar structure in EBMed Ti-6Al-4 V was associated with the epitaxial solidification of the prior β phase. From a crystallographic perspective, the cubic β phase preferentially grows along the < 100 > directions, which are easy growth axes for BCC crystals. Because the highest thermal gradient aligns with the Z axis, grains with their [001] orientation parallel to the build direction dominate. This crystallographic alignment preserves the β-to-α transformation, resulting in mechanical anisotropies [ 132 ,  133 ].

sections.heading: Direct energy deposition process (DED)
paragraphs: This process was one of the frequently employed techniques for printing metal alloys. In this process, the laser is the key component for fusing the metal powder according to the G-codes generated by the corresponding software. The microstructure obtained by the DED process was influenced by rapid solidification, cooling conditions, and associated phase transformations. Nevertheless, the availability of metal alloys suitable for 3D printing remains limited, with only a small selection available in powder or wire form [ 134 ]. In the DED process, material is deposited and built up layer by layer from the base upward. This technique is primarily utilised for component repair, the fabrication of complex metallic structures, and cladding for coating. Compared with conventional methods, titanium alloy parts produced by DED typically exhibit reduced ductility and increased strength under constant processing parameters [ 135 ]. The working process of the DED process is depicted in Fig.  21 .
Fig. 21 Illustration of the DED technique [ 136 ]

Various studies were conducted during this process to achieve better microstructure and mechanical properties based on optimized parameters. J. Alexis et al. reported that pausing between layers influences microstructure and mechanical properties. Coarse α plates were obtained, which tend to lower the material’s tensile strength [ 137 ]. The DED process has the highest cooling condition, leading to an α’ martensitic phase that reduces the material’s ductility; this can be improved through further heat treatment. Various heat treatment conditions were tested, and their microstructural evolution is shown in Fig.  22 , illustrating the transformation from a columnar grain to an equiaxed grain structure. Among the cooling conditions, furnace cooling appears most promising, as it produces a thermodynamically stable lamellar α + β structure by eliminating the martensitic α’ structure, which results in a slight decrease in hardness but a significant improvement in ductility [ 138 ].
Fig. 22 DEDed processed Ti-6Al-4 V ( a ) as built, Heat treated at 1050 °C and cooling conditions follow - ( b ) annealing, ( c ) normalising, ( d ) water quenching [ 138 ]

sections.heading: Processing – structure – property relation in additive manufacturing
paragraphs: Synthesizing Ti-6Al-4V through additive manufacturing can achieve a relative density of around 99%. The performance of the material depends on how it cools from the molten state [ 18 ]. In selective laser melting, a laser rapidly melts the powder, which then cools at an extremely high rate. This rapid cooling tends to the needle-like or acicular α’ martensite structure [ 139 ]. This structure provides high tensile strength and low ductility [ 140 ]. Consequently, post-processing treatment was required to transform the martensitic phase into the stable α + β phase, which may increase ductility and reduce residual stress [ 141 ]. In contrast, the electron beam melting maintains a high bed temperature, which tends to anneal the sample while synthesising, allowing the metastable martensite to transform into an α + β lamellar structure [ 111 ,  142 ]. As a result, the EBM-processed component exhibits improved ductility and fracture toughness compared to SLM, although achievable strength may be reduced due to grain coarsening. In directed energy deposition experiences intermediate cooling rates producing a mixture of α and α’ with elongated β grains. Due to the large melt pools and layer-by-layer deposition, this process exhibits anisotropy [ 143 ]. The mechanical properties would vary with the build and scanning directions due to elongated β grains [ 144 ]. From a practical perspective, each AM technique offers distinct advantages for different applications. SLM may be particularly suitable for smaller and more critically complex materials. Whereas EBM may be suitable where ductility is necessary. In contrast, DED is well-suited for large structural components due to its high deposition rate. Although its geometric accuracy may be less or more anisotropic. Therefore, the suitable AM technique would be determined by the balance among microstructure, size, geometric complexity, and material strength. sections.heading: Comparison between conventional and additive powder metallurgy techniques
paragraphs: The consolidation of Ti-6Al-4 V through powder-based routes can be categorised into two: conventional and additive manufacturing. Both differed in their thermal cycles and densification kinetics. The conventional routes require a longer duration of thermal exposure to attain their final density, which would lead to a coarser microstructure, and the mechanical performance would be commensurate with it. This makes the conventional route predictable and suitable for mass production. In contrast to the conventional route, additive manufacturing achieves full density because the precursor is fully melted. In this route, a very fine-grained material can be obtained, thereby enhancing mechanical performance. During this process, the material experiences directional heat flow, leading to columnar grain growth. Therefore, the AM route provides better mechanical performance and offers design freedom, but it requires post-processing to achieve a stable microstructure, as the conventional route would naturally have. From a cost perspective, powder metallurgy techniques have lower production costs in large-scale manufacturing than AM. The equipment which was required for the AM process is expensive. Other than that, a higher energy input is also required, which will increase production costs. The metal powders used in AM techniques are more expensive due to the strict requirements for particle size distribution and morphology [ 156 ]. However, the AM offers advantages for complex geometries that are difficult to fabricate using conventional routes. Table  8  depicts the overall difference between the two routes.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This review reports the influence of different powder metallurgical processing techniques on densification, microstructural characteristics, and mechanical behaviour, as well as the effects of processing parameters on the Ti-6Al-4 V alloy. The key findings from the reviewed studies are summarised as follows:

Among the reported routes, MIM and conventional methods required more time to densify the material and were difficult to achieve maximum density and the desired phase in the material. Compared to MIM and traditional sintering, microwave sintering processes the material quickly. The literature shows it can achieve a finer microstructure, but uneven densification may occur due to the parameters. The SPS process allows rapid densification quickly while preventing grain growth, making it more efficient than traditional sintering methods. Careful selection of processing parameters and suitable powder characteristics enables the achievement of higher density, controlled microstructure, desired phase composition, and enhanced mechanical properties. In additive manufacturing, optimising processing parameters to achieve high density and a refined microstructure allows Ti-6Al-4 V to exhibit mechanical properties comparable to, and in certain instances exceeding, those obtained through traditional manufacturing routes. However, removing the α′ martensitic phase, which typically forms during processing, remains a major challenge and often requires additional post-processing treatments.

Overall, powder metallurgy offers versatile ways to customize Ti–6Al–4 V properties for specific engineering needs. While notable progress has been made in optimizing densification and microstructural control, challenges still exist in achieving uniform phase distribution and balancing strength and ductility. Future research should focus on advanced sintering techniques and alloying additions to improve the alloy’s mechanical reliability and application potential in aerospace, biomedical, and structural applications.
